Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Canadian ski resort gondola cars that were left dangling and swaying with terrified skiers inside failed because ice buildup snapped a supporting tower, the resort said Thursday. One gondola car is suspended above an icy creek at a ski resort near Whistler, British Columbia. In a rare occurrence called ice-jacking, water seeped into the lower section of the lift tower and turned to ice Tuesday at Whistler Blackcomb resort, 177 kilometers (110 miles) north of Vancouver, a resort official said in a press release Thursday. The lift hangs from a tower that is spliced into two parts. Extremely cold temperatures caused the ice buildup that exerted 800 tons of pressure between the two parts that hold the tower together, causing them to rupture, according to Whistler Blackcomb. The section of the lift affected by the accident had 15 cars going up the mountain and 15 coming down at the time, but they weren't carrying a lot of passengers, according to Doug Forseth, senior vice president of the resort. He said 53 passengers had been rescued from the stranded cars. No skiers at the Whistler, British Columbia, resort were seriously injured. "The towers are not normally designed to allow for any water penetration and so this failure is a very unusual situation," said Warren Sparks, senior vice president of Doppelmayr Canada, the engineering firm that investigated the accident. They are trying to figure out what caused the water to pool. He said independent structural engineers are examining the tower from Vancouver-based CVMM Consulting Engineers. "The evidence so far indicates a sudden rupture rather than a fatigue failure over an extended period," Sparks said. At least two gondola cars broke away and hit the ground, both from relatively low heights near the tower that split, and caused the system's heavy cable line to slacken, according to Tyler Noble, a reporter for CNNRadio affiliate CKNW in Vancouver. "One hit a bus stop and the other hit a house," Noble said Wednesday. "Another one was suspended over a creek, but everyone is out of that car." The broken Excaliber Gondola was not operating Thursday. Whistler engineers checked eight similar towers across the two mountains of the resort. All passed those inspections, and are open Thursday, the release said. The British Columbia Authority says it does not expect to rescind operating permits on any lifts at the resort, other than the Excaliber Gondola. Jeff Colburn, general manager of Silver Mountain Resort in Kellogg, Idaho, said a lift tower at his resort was similarly damaged by ice in December 2006. The damage was discovered in the morning before the slopes opened, so no one was endangered, he said. The damaged tower was replaced in about three weeks, Colburn said, and the resort's business was not significantly disrupted. "We check our towers in the summer now, and we also check before we open up for ski season as well just to make sure they don't have any water in them, and we've worked with the manufacturers," he said. Holes have been drilled in the bases of towers so that water can drain out, Colburn said. CNN's Ashley Fantz and Jim Kavanagh contributed to this report.

(CNN) -- Gondola cabins at a Canadian ski resort were left hanging and rocking with frightened skiers trapped inside after ice accumulation broke a support tower, resort officials announced Thursday. Near Whistler, British Columbia, one gondola cabin remained suspended over a frozen creek at the resort.

According to a resort statement released Thursday, an unusual phenomenon known as ice-jacking occurred at Whistler Blackcomb resort, located 177 kilometers (110 miles) north of Vancouver. On Tuesday, water penetrated the bottom portion of the lift tower and froze solid.

The tower supporting the lift is joined together in two pieces. Whistler Blackcomb explained that severe cold conditions produced the ice accumulation, which generated 800 tons of force between the two connected sections, ultimately breaking them apart.

Doug Forseth, the resort's senior vice president, noted that when the incident happened, the affected part of the lift had 15 cabins ascending the mountain and another 15 descending, though passenger numbers were low. He reported that 53 people had been pulled to safety from the trapped cabins. None of the skiers at the British Columbia resort suffered serious harm.

Warren Sparks, senior vice president of Doppelmayr Canada—the engineering company that looked into the incident—stated, "The towers are not normally designed to allow for any water penetration and so this failure is a very unusual situation." Investigators are still working to determine how the water accumulated. Sparks added that separate structural engineers from Vancouver's CVMM Consulting Engineers are inspecting the tower.

"The evidence so far indicates a sudden rupture rather than a fatigue failure over an extended period," Sparks said.

Tyler Noble, a journalist with CNNRadio affiliate CKNW in Vancouver, reported that a minimum of two gondola cabins detached and struck the ground. Both fell from fairly low positions close to the tower that fractured, which caused the system's massive cable to go slack.

"One hit a bus stop and the other hit a house," Noble reported Wednesday. "Another one was suspended over a creek, but everyone is out of that car."

The damaged Excaliber Gondola remained shut down Thursday. Whistler engineers inspected eight comparable towers spread across the resort's two mountains. According to the statement, every one of them passed inspection and reopened Thursday. The British Columbia Authority indicated it does not anticipate revoking operating permits for any of the resort's lifts, with the exception of the Excaliber Gondola.

Jeff Colburn, who manages Silver Mountain Resort in Kellogg, Idaho, recounted that a lift tower at his facility sustained similar ice damage in December 2006. He explained that staff spotted the damage in the morning before the slopes opened, meaning no one was put at risk. Colburn said crews replaced the damaged tower within roughly three weeks, and the incident didn't seriously affect the resort's operations.

"We check our towers in the summer now, and we also check before we open up for ski season as well just to make sure they don't have any water in them, and we've worked with the manufacturers," he said. Colburn added that holes were bored into the bottoms of the towers to allow water to escape.

CNN's Ashley Fantz and Jim Kavanagh contributed to this report.

As the water froze and expanded within the tower, the resulting ice buildup exerted an astonishing 800 tons of pressure between the two spliced sections of the structure. This immense force ultimately caused the sections to rupture at the point where they had been joined together.

# Ski Lift Tower Ruptures at BC Resort Amid Extreme Cold; No Serious Injuries Reported

**BRITISH COLUMBIA** — A ski lift tower fractured at a British Columbia mountain resort early this morning after a prolonged deep freeze and mounting ice pressure compromised the structure's integrity, resort officials confirmed. Despite the dramatic failure, no serious injuries have been reported.

## What Happened

The incident occurred shortly after the lift opened for the day, when a support tower on one of the resort's primary chairlifts buckled under conditions that had gripped the region for nearly a week. Overnight temperatures had plunged to approximately -35°C, with wind chill values dropping significantly lower.

Witnesses described hearing a sharp cracking sound before lift operators immediately engaged emergency braking systems and halted the lift.

"We heard what sounded like a gunshot, then everything stopped," said one skier who was on the lift at the time. "The staff got everyone down calmly. They knew exactly what to do."

Resort ski patrol and mechanical crews executed a rope-rescue evacuation, safely lowering approximately two dozen guests suspended along the line. The process took roughly two hours, with all guests reaching the ground without incident. A small number were assessed for cold exposure but declined further medical attention.

## The Role of Extreme Cold

Engineers point to a combination of factors that likely contributed to the failure.

"Steel becomes more brittle in extreme cold," explained a structural engineer specializing in alpine infrastructure. "At sub -30 conditions, the metal loses some of its ductility—its ability to flex under stress. When you combine that with accumulated ice loading and thermal contraction, you create conditions where a structure that normally has significant safety margins can experience localized failure."

Ice accretion is believed to have added substantial weight and stress to the tower. Freeze-thaw cycles earlier in the season may also have introduced moisture into micro-fractures, which then expanded upon freezing—a process known as ice wedging that can progressively weaken steel and its connection points.

"This is a textbook example of how compounding environmental stressors behave," the engineer added. "No single factor may have caused this alone, but stacked together, they exceeded the tower's tolerance."

## Resort Response

The resort has closed the affected lift indefinitely and launched a full investigation in coordination with technical safety authorities. Other lifts at the resort remain operational following precautionary inspections.

"The safety of our guests and staff is our absolute priority," a resort spokesperson said in a statement. "Our team responded exactly as trained, and we're grateful everyone is safe. We will not reopen this lift until it has been fully inspected, repaired, and certified."

Technical Safety BC, the provincial body overseeing lift infrastructure, is expected to conduct an independent review of the failure.

## Broader Concerns

The incident has renewed discussions about aging mountain infrastructure and the challenges posed by increasingly volatile winter weather.

"We're seeing wider temperature swings and more extreme events," noted a mountain operations consultant. "Infrastructure built decades ago was engineered for a certain envelope of conditions. Operators across the industry are having to reassess maintenance schedules and cold-weather protocols."

Experts recommend that resorts implement enhanced monitoring during extreme cold snaps, including more frequent structural inspections and temperature-based operating thresholds.

## What's Next

The resort has committed to providing updates as the investigation proceeds. Guests holding affected passes are being offered alternative access and accommodations.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*
